span: Section 18 of Mcoca through a non obstante clause overrides the mandate contained in Sections 25 and 26 of the Evidence Act, by rendering a confession as admissible, even if it is made to a police officer
why: Court relies on MCOCA s.18 to hold that confessions to senior police officers are admissible despite ss.25-26; its own sentence says their value cannot be ignored.

span: such portion alone would be admissible under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, and not the entire confessional statements
why: Headnote: confessions to police are barred but the part leading to recovery is admissible under s.27.

span: It is trite that confession of an accused recorded by a Police Officer is not admissible in evidence as the same is hit by Section 25 of the Evidence Act
why: Headnote holding that a police-recorded confession is inadmissible under s.25.

span: the confessional statement was not by the respondent
why: Concerns use of others' confessions as evidence in a bank's departmental inquiry, a different condition from admissibility in a criminal trial.

span: Only so much of information as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered is admissible
why: Headnote on s.27: only the part of a custodial statement leading to discovery is admissible, which partly admits and partly excludes a statement to police.

span: under Section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872; a confessional statement given by an accused before a Police officer is inadmissible as evidence
why: Headnote holding: lower courts erred in relying on statements made to the police because s.25 makes them inadmissible.

span: Statement given under Section 161, even if relevant, as it contains an admission, would not be admissible
why: Court reasons that statements to police during investigation are barred by s.162, and the next paragraph states that a confession to a police officer is clearly inadmissible.

span: any confessional statement made to such officers, would be barred u/s. 25
why: Headnote holding: officers with s.53 NDPS powers are police officers, so confessions to them are barred by s.25 and not substantive evidence.
